title: Prompt, RAG or Fine-Tune: Choosing the Right LLM Customization
summary: Quick revision notes on deciding between prompting, RAG and fine-tuning, how full fine-tuning compares to LoRA/PEFT, data and cost needs, distillation, and picking model size. Ends with a decision cheat sheet.

chapters.title: The Customization Ladder
points: Prompting changes instructions at inference: zero cost to start, instant to iterate, but limited by context window and model's existing skills
RAG retrieves documents at query time and injects them into the prompt: fixes missing or changing knowledge, gives citations, no weight changes
Fine-tuning updates weights: fixes behavior, style, format and domain skill, but is poor at injecting fresh facts
Rule of thumb: knowledge gap -> RAG; behavior/format gap -> fine-tune; neither -> better prompt. Always try prompting first
Interview Point: Why not fine-tune to add company docs? When would you combine RAG and fine-tuning? How do you decide with a failing eval?

chapters.title: Choosing Between Prompt, RAG and Fine-Tune
points: Decision order: baseline prompt + few-shot -> add RAG if facts missing/stale -> fine-tune if behavior still fails or latency/cost needs a smaller model
Comparison row: data freshness (RAG best), style/format consistency (fine-tune best), setup effort (prompt < RAG < fine-tune), per-query cost (fine-tune can shrink prompts)
Fine-tune wins when: strict output format, tone, narrow classification/extraction at high volume, or replacing long few-shot prompts to cut tokens
RAG wins when: data changes often, answers need source citations, access control per user, or corpus is too large for context
Interview Point: Support bot with weekly-changing policies: which approach and why? How do you measure whether fine-tuning beat prompting? Can long context replace RAG?

chapters.title: Full Fine-Tuning vs LoRA and PEFT
points: Full fine-tuning updates all weights: needs memory for weights + gradients + optimizer states (Adam ~ 12-16 bytes/param in mixed precision), so a 7B model needs ~100 GB+
PEFT trains a small set of extra params and freezes the base model; LoRA adds low-rank matrices W + BA with rank r (typically 8-64), training under 1% of params
QLoRA = LoRA on a 4-bit quantized base model: a 7B fits on one 16-24 GB GPU; small quality loss versus 16-bit LoRA
LoRA adapters are small (MBs), swappable per task/customer, and can be merged into base weights for zero extra inference latency; full FT yields a full model copy per task
Key knobs: rank r, alpha (scaling, often 2r), target modules (attention q,v or all linear layers), learning rate (LoRA ~1e-4 to 2e-4, higher than full FT's ~1e-5)
Interview Point: Why does low rank work? LoRA vs QLoRA trade-off? When is full fine-tuning still worth it?

chapters.title: Data Needs, Costs and Distillation
points: Data: quality beats quantity; hundreds to a few thousand clean, diverse examples often suffice for style/format with LoRA; new skills or domains need tens of thousands+
Format matters: instruction/response pairs or chat-format JSONL, consistent with the inference prompt template; hold out 10-20% as eval set

Cost drivers: training = tokens x epochs x model size (LoRA mainly cuts GPU memory; compute drops only modestly, since no gradients are computed for the frozen weights); hidden costs are data labeling, eval and re-training on each base-model upgrade
Serving cost: hosted fine-tuned models often cost more per token than base; self-hosted merged LoRA adds no overhead; multi-adapter serving shares one base

Distillation: a large teacher model generates labeled outputs (or soft logits) to train a small student, giving near-teacher quality on a narrow task at far lower latency and cost; check teacher license terms
Interview Point: How many examples do you need? What does distillation cost versus save? How do you build a synthetic dataset safely?

chapters.title: Choosing Model Size and Common Mistakes
points: Size trade-off: bigger = better reasoning and fewer failures, but higher latency, cost and memory (fp16 needs ~2 GB per 1B params, 4-bit ~0.5 GB, plus KV cache)
Pick procedure: start with the strongest model to prove feasibility, then step down until the eval metric drops below target; small fine-tuned models often beat large prompted ones on narrow tasks
Mistake: fine-tuning to add knowledge instead of RAG, causing hallucinated facts and stale answers
Mistake: no eval set or baseline, so you cannot tell if fine-tuning helped; also training on noisy, duplicated or test-leaking data
Mistake: over-training causing catastrophic forgetting and overfitting; fix with fewer epochs, lower LR, lower rank or mixing in general data
Interview Point: How do you choose the smallest sufficient model? What is catastrophic forgetting? How do you detect overfitting in fine-tuning?

chapters.title: Customization Cheat Sheet
points: Gap type: missing/changing facts -> RAG; wrong style/format/behavior -> fine-tune; unclear task -> improve prompt and few-shot
Order of effort: prompt -> RAG -> LoRA/QLoRA -> full fine-tune; combine RAG + fine-tune for domain behavior plus fresh facts
LoRA defaults: r 8-16, alpha 2r, all linear layers, LR 1e-4 to 2e-4, 1-3 epochs; QLoRA to fit 7B in ~16 GB
Data: 100s-1000s clean examples for style, 10k+ for new skills; hold out an eval set and keep a prompt-only baseline
Cut cost with: distillation to a small student, merged adapters, smaller model that still meets the eval bar
